paragraphs.heading: A rising column of hot rock
paragraphs.text: A mantle plume is a proposed kind of convection inside Earth's mantle. The idea is that extremely hot material gathers at the boundary between the core and the mantle and then rises up through the mantle. It was put forward to explain volcanism that does not fit the usual pattern. J. Tuzo Wilson first proposed plumes in 1963, and W. Jason Morgan developed the idea in 1971 and 1972.

paragraphs.heading: Why geologists invoke them
paragraphs.text: When the top of a plume reaches shallow depths, it partly melts. That is why plumes are often blamed for volcanic hotspots such as Hawaii and Iceland. The Deccan and Siberian Traps, two large igneous provinces, are tied to them as well. Some of these volcanic areas sit far from the edges of tectonic plates, while others are unusually large eruptions close to plate edges.

paragraphs.heading: Shaped like a mushroom
paragraphs.text: In the early 1970s, researchers mimicked plumes with small tanks of fluid in the laboratory. From those tests, a plume is pictured as two parts: a long, thin pipe called a conduit, and a rounded head that grows as the plume climbs. Together they look like a mushroom. The head swells because hot material moves up the conduit faster than the whole plume can push up through the rock around it.

paragraphs.heading: When the head arrives
paragraphs.text: When a plume head meets the base of the lithosphere, it is expected to spread flat against it. It should then go through widespread decompression melting, making large volumes of basalt magma that may erupt at the surface. These eruptions have been tied to flood basalts, such as the Deccan Traps in India and the Columbia River basalts of North America. Flood basalts on the ocean floor are called oceanic plateaus, like the Ontong Java Plateau in the western Pacific.

paragraphs.heading: Chains of volcanoes
paragraphs.text: The thin conduit is thought to keep feeding magma to a hotspot. If the plume stays put while a plate slides over it, the eruptions should build a line of volcanoes running in the direction the plate moves. The Hawaiian Islands are the classic case. Yet recent work found that the volcanic centre of the Hawaiian chain has itself shifted over time.

paragraphs.heading: A debated idea
paragraphs.text: Basalts erupted at hotspots differ subtly in their chemistry from the basalts of mid-ocean ridges. That signature comes from material that once lay near the surface, such as subducted slabs and continental sediments, being mixed into the mantle source. In the plume view, that material was carried down to the core-mantle boundary and then brought back up by plumes. In a rival view, called the Plate hypothesis, the material mostly cycles through the shallow mantle and volcanoes tap it there.
